items.summary: Philosophy of race is the area of philosophy that examines the concept of race, asking whether races are biologically real, socially constructed, or should be eliminated from our conceptual scheme, and analyzing the moral and political implications of racial categories. The field is commonly framed around three broad positions: racial naturalism, social constructionism about race, and racial anti-realism or eliminativism. It draws on metaphysics, philosophy of biology, philosophy of language, and ethics, and overlaps with critical philosophy of race and with debates over racism, identity, and justice.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — The Concept of Race in Science and Philosophy / Race

items.rationale: Defines the field neutrally as an academic area of study (not a claim about race itself), names the standard three-way taxonomy of positions (naturalism / constructionism / anti-realism), and notes its parent disciplines — all standard-reference content. Flag for QC: the SEP has an entry titled 'Race' (slug likely 'race'); confirm the exact slug and that it covers the naturalism/constructionism/anti-realism taxonomy. IEP slug 'race' is my best guess and should be verified.

items.summary: Philosophy of cognitive science is the branch of philosophy that examines the foundations, methods, and central concepts of the interdisciplinary study of the mind, drawing on psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, artificial intelligence, and philosophy of mind. Recurring questions concern the nature of mental representation and computation, whether cognition is best modeled by symbolic rules, connectionist networks, or dynamical and embodied approaches, and how the study of the mind relates to the brain. It overlaps substantially with philosophy of mind and philosophy of psychology, and addresses methodological issues such as the levels at which cognitive phenomena should be explained.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — The Computational Theory of Mind / Cognitive Science
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Cognitive Science / Philosophy of Mind

items.rationale: Defines the field by its recognized scope (foundations/methods of cognitive science), names canonical debates (representation/computation, symbolic vs. connectionist vs. embodied/dynamical), and notes overlap with philosophy of mind/psychology — all standard. Flag for QC: SEP has an entry 'Cognitive Science' (verify slug 'cognitive-science'); IEP slug uncertain — verify whether IEP has a dedicated 'cognitive-science' entry or whether the anchor content lives under 'Philosophy of Mind'.

items.summary: Media and communication studies is an academic discipline concerned with the content, history, institutions, and effects of communication and mass media, encompassing the study of how messages are produced, transmitted, and interpreted across interpersonal, organizational, and mass channels. The field draws on the social sciences and humanities, integrating theories from sociology, psychology, political science, cultural studies, and rhetoric, and examines print, broadcast, film, and digital media. It emerged as a distinct academic area over the twentieth century and includes subfields such as mass communication, media effects research, and cultural and critical media studies.
items.rationale: Defines the field by recognized scope (content/institutions/effects of media and communication), names its interdisciplinary sources and media types, and gives an uncontroversial historical anchor (20th-century emergence). No SEP/IEP entry expected for this field; hints are Britannica + Wikipedia. Flag for QC: verify the Britannica 'communication' topic page and the two Wikipedia articles support the interdisciplinary-sources and 20th-century-emergence claims.

items.summary: Physical anthropology, also known as biological anthropology, is the subfield of anthropology that studies humans as a biological species, including human evolution, genetic variation, growth and adaptation, primatology, and the fossil record of human ancestors. It applies the methods of biology and the earth sciences to questions about human origins and diversity, and encompasses areas such as paleoanthropology, human osteology, and forensic anthropology. The discipline is generally regarded as one of the traditional major branches of anthropology alongside cultural, linguistic, and archaeological anthropology.

source_hints.source: American Association of Biological Anthropologists — About

items.rationale: Defines the subfield by recognized scope (human evolution, variation, primatology, fossil record), notes the synonym 'biological anthropology', names its sub-areas, and places it among the four traditional branches of anthropology — standard content. Flag for QC: verify the AABA 'about' URL (organization renamed from AAPA to AABA); Britannica page slug 'physical-anthropology' should be confirmed.

items.summary: Mass communication is the study of how messages are transmitted to large, dispersed, and heterogeneous audiences through mass media such as newspapers, radio, television, film, and digital platforms. As an academic subfield it examines media institutions, message production and content, audiences, and effects, and includes influential theoretical traditions such as agenda-setting, cultivation, uses-and-gratifications, and framing. It is closely associated with media and communication studies and with journalism, and is often distinguished from interpersonal communication by the scale and mediated character of its channels.
items.rationale: Defines the subfield by recognized scope (transmission to large dispersed audiences via mass media), names canonical theoretical traditions (agenda-setting, cultivation, uses-and-gratifications, framing), and its relation to communication studies/journalism — standard content. Flag for QC: confirm the named theories are attributed as mass-communication traditions in the cited sources; verify the Britannica 'mass-communication' slug.

items.summary: Psychoanalysis is a body of theory and a set of clinical methods for treating mental disorders, founded by Sigmund Freud in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, centered on the idea that unconscious mental processes shape thought, emotion, and behavior. Its core concepts include the unconscious, repression, transference, free association, and the interpretation of dreams, together with structural models of the mind such as the division into id, ego, and superego. As an intellectual tradition it gave rise to numerous later schools associated with figures such as Carl Jung, Melanie Klein, and Jacques Lacan, and it has influenced psychology, psychiatry, and the humanities while also drawing sustained scientific and philosophical criticism.

source_hints.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Sigmund Freud
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Philosophy of Psychiatry / related entries

items.rationale: Defines psychoanalysis by scope (theory + clinical method), attributes its founding to Freud (uncontroversial), names core concepts and the id/ego/superego model, names major later schools, and notes both influence and criticism conservatively. Flag for QC: SEP may not have a standalone 'Freud' entry (slug 'freud' uncertain) — the SEP hint may need to point to a different entry; verify. All named figures (Jung, Klein, Lacan) are deceased; no living-person concern.

items.summary: The Internet is the global system of interconnected computer networks that communicate using the standardized Internet protocol suite (TCP/IP), linking devices and networks worldwide and carrying a broad range of information resources and services. It originated in packet-switching research of the 1960s and the ARPANET, funded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency, with the TCP/IP protocols developed in the 1970s enabling the interconnection of heterogeneous networks. The Internet is commonly distinguished from the World Wide Web, an information system of linked hypertext documents and other resources that runs over it. It underpins applications such as electronic mail, file transfer, and the Web, and its technical standards are coordinated by bodies including the Internet Engineering Task Force.

source_hints.source: Internet Society — Brief History of the Internet

items.rationale: Defines the Internet by its technical nature (interconnected networks using TCP/IP), gives the uncontroversial ARPANET/packet-switching origin, distinguishes it from the Web, and names the IETF for standards — all standard-reference content. Flag for QC: verify the Internet Society 'brief-history' URL is live (long-standing page, but confirm the path); confirm Britannica slug 'Internet'.

items.summary: Structural anthropology is an approach in anthropology, most closely associated with Claude Lévi-Strauss, that analyzes culture as a system of underlying structures modeled on the relational and binary logic of structural linguistics. It holds that phenomena such as myth, kinship, and classification can be understood as expressions of universal patterns of the human mind, particularly binary oppositions and their transformations. Developed principally in the mid-twentieth century, it drew on the linguistics of Ferdinand de Saussure and Roman Jakobson and was highly influential across the social sciences and humanities before being challenged by post-structuralist and other later critiques.

source_hints.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Structuralism / Ferdinand de Saussure

items.rationale: Defines the approach by its method (culture as underlying relational/binary structures on the model of structural linguistics), attributes it chiefly to Lévi-Strauss, names its linguistic sources (Saussure, Jakobson), and notes its mid-20th-century development and later post-structuralist critique — standard content, all figures deceased. Flag for QC: the IEP slug 'structuralism-in-anthropology' is my best guess and may not exist — verify or substitute an IEP entry that covers structuralism; Britannica hint points to the Lévi-Strauss biography as anchor.

items.summary: Logical positivism, also called logical empiricism, was a philosophical movement that flourished in the 1920s and 1930s, most prominently among members of the Vienna Circle and associated thinkers in Berlin. It combined empiricism with the tools of modern formal logic and held that meaningful statements are either analytic truths of logic and mathematics or empirically verifiable claims, treating metaphysical and much traditional philosophical discourse as cognitively meaningless on the strength of a verifiability criterion of meaning. Central figures included Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, and Otto Neurath, with A. J. Ayer helping popularize the view in the English-speaking world. The movement declined after the 1930s under internal difficulties with the verifiability criterion and external criticism, but strongly shaped the development of analytic philosophy and philosophy of science.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — The Vienna Circle / Logical Empiricism
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Logical Positivism / Vienna Circle

items.rationale: Well-established history only: dates (1920s-30s), the analytic/verifiable dichotomy and verifiability criterion, the association with the Vienna Circle, canonical figures (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath, Ayer), and its decline and influence on analytic philosophy/philosophy of science. All figures deceased. Flag for QC: SEP entry is titled 'The Vienna Circle' or 'Logical Empiricism' — verify the correct slug (I used 'logical-empiricism'); IEP slug 'logical-positivism' should be confirmed.

items.summary: Generative grammar is an approach to the study of language, originating with the work of Noam Chomsky in the 1950s, that seeks to specify a finite system of explicit rules capable of generating all and only the grammatical sentences of a language. It treats grammar as a formal system representing the tacit linguistic knowledge, or competence, of an idealized native speaker, and is associated with the hypothesis of an innate universal grammar shared across human languages. The framework has passed through successive formulations, including transformational grammar, government-and-binding theory, and the Minimalist Program, and has been influential in linguistics and cognitive science while remaining contested among competing theoretical approaches.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Noam Chomsky / Philosophy of Linguistics

items.rationale: Defines the approach by its aim (finite rule system generating grammatical sentences), attributes origin to Chomsky in the 1950s, names the competence notion and universal-grammar hypothesis, and lists the standard historical stages (transformational, GB, Minimalism), with a conservative 'contested' note. Flag for QC: Chomsky is living, but he is named only as originator of a well-documented theory (standard attributed historical claim, no biographical/reputational content) — this is the only living-figure mention in the batch; QC should confirm the wording stays to the uncontested historical attribution. Verify SEP 'chomsky' slug and Britannica 'generative-grammar' slug.

items.summary: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a class of cryptographic systems that use pairs of related keys, a public key that may be shared openly and a private key kept secret, so that operations performed with one key can only be reversed with the other. It enables secure communication and digital signatures without requiring the parties to share a secret key in advance, addressing the key-distribution problem of symmetric cryptography. The concept was introduced publicly by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, and the widely used RSA algorithm was described by Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman shortly afterward; its security typically rests on computational problems such as integer factorization or discrete logarithms.
items.rationale: Defines the concept by its mechanism (asymmetric key pairs, public/private) and function (secure communication + signatures, solving key distribution), and gives the well-documented public-invention history (Diffie-Hellman 1976; RSA by Rivest-Shamir-Adleman). Note some inventors may be living; they are named only as authors of a documented 1976-77 result (standard historical attribution, no biographical claims). Flag for QC: Britannica may cover this under 'cryptology' rather than a dedicated page — verify the anchor; confirm the 1976 Diffie-Hellman date and RSA attribution in the cited sources.

items.summary: Analysis of algorithms is the area of computer science concerned with determining the computational resources, chiefly running time and memory, required to execute an algorithm, typically as a function of the size of its input. It commonly characterizes efficiency using asymptotic notation such as big-O, and distinguishes worst-case, average-case, and best-case behavior. The systematic study of algorithmic efficiency is closely associated with Donald Knuth, whose multi-volume work The Art of Computer Programming helped establish the field, and it provides the analytical foundation for computational complexity theory and for comparing algorithms independently of particular machines.

source_hints.source: Britannica — Analysis of algorithms / Computer science
Wikipedia — The Art of Computer Programming

items.rationale: Defines the field by scope (resource requirements as a function of input size), names asymptotic notation and the worst/average/best-case distinction, and associates it with Knuth and The Art of Computer Programming (standard, well-documented). Knuth is living but named only as author of a documented foundational work — uncontested historical attribution, no biographical/reputational content. Flag for QC: Britannica likely covers this within the broader 'computer science' article rather than a dedicated page — verify the anchor; confirm the Knuth/TAOCP association in the cited sources.

items.summary: Behavioral economics is a subfield of economics that incorporates insights from psychology into the analysis of economic decision-making, studying how cognitive limitations, biases, and social and emotional factors lead people to depart systematically from the predictions of standard rational-choice models. It draws heavily on the work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky on judgment under uncertainty and prospect theory, and on later contributions to topics such as bounded rationality, framing effects, and self-control. The field applies these findings to areas including finance, public policy, and consumer behavior, and is closely related to behavioral finance.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Philosophy of Economics

items.rationale: Defines the subfield by scope (psychology + economic decision-making, systematic departures from rational-choice models), names its canonical foundation (Kahneman & Tversky, prospect theory) and standard topics (bounded rationality, framing, self-control), and its applications. Kahneman was living recently; he is named only for the well-documented prospect-theory contribution (standard attribution) — QC should confirm wording is purely the historical/intellectual attribution. Flag for QC: verify Britannica 'behavioral-economics' slug; SEP 'economics' entry is the philosophy-of-economics anchor.

items.summary: Social choice theory is a field at the intersection of economics, political science, and philosophy that studies how individual preferences, judgments, or welfare can be aggregated into a collective decision or social ranking. Its modern form was shaped by Kenneth Arrow, whose impossibility theorem showed that no aggregation rule can simultaneously satisfy a set of apparently reasonable fairness conditions, and by later work associated with Amartya Sen and others on welfare, rights, and measurement. The field encompasses voting theory, welfare economics, and the analysis of fairness and collective rationality, and has close ties to game theory and to normative debates about democracy and distributive justice.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Social Choice Theory / Arrow's Theorem
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Social Choice Theory
Britannica — Social choice theory / Kenneth Arrow

items.rationale: Defines the field by scope (aggregation of individual preferences into collective decisions), anchors it in Arrow's impossibility theorem and later welfare/rights work (Sen), and names its component areas (voting theory, welfare economics, fairness) and ties to game theory. Arrow is deceased; Sen is living but named only for a documented intellectual contribution (standard attribution). items.summary: The Vienna Circle (German: Wiener Kreis) was a group of philosophers, scientists, and mathematicians who met in Vienna from the 1920s until the mid-1930s, gathering around the philosopher Moritz Schlick, and was the principal center of the movement known as logical positivism or logical empiricism. Its members and associates, who included Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath, Hans Hahn, and (more loosely) figures such as Kurt Gödel, sought to develop a scientifically grounded philosophy using modern logic and to eliminate metaphysics, a program set out in the 1929 manifesto commonly titled The Scientific Conception of the World. The Circle dispersed in the 1930s amid the political upheaval of the period and the assassination of Schlick in 1936, with many members emigrating and carrying its influence into analytic philosophy and philosophy of science abroad.

source_hints.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — The Vienna Circle
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Vienna Circle / Logical Positivism

items.rationale: Well-established history only: the group's Vienna meetings (1920s-mid-1930s), its formation around Schlick, its identity as the center of logical positivism, canonical members (Carnap, Neurath, Hahn; Gödel loosely associated), the 1929 manifesto, and the dispersal amid 1930s politics and Schlick's 1936 assassination. All figures deceased. Flag for QC: verify SEP slug 'vienna-circle' and IEP slug 'vienna-circle' (best guesses); confirm the 1929 manifesto title and Schlick assassination year (1936) in the cited sources.
